title: A-M-N

lines: MOSES ON THE HILL, HANDS RAISED.
cards: The battle is under way. Moses stands on a hill above it with his hands raised, and the story says that while his hands are up, Israel prevails; when they drop, Amalek prevails. Arms get heavy.

So Aaron and Hur bring a stone for him to sit on, and stand one on each side, holding his hands up. Then comes a phrase that sounds like a small detail: "his hands were steady until the going down of the sun."
The Hebrew behind steady is emunah, the same word elsewhere translated as faith. Today's three letters live inside it.

teach.b: A-M-N. Alef, mem, nun. Turn it four ways.
First, steadiness. In the Moses story, emunah describes hands that don't waver, and they don't waver because friends are holding them. Faith here isn't an opinion.
It's something that holds. Second, amen. The same letters give the word said in answer to a blessing.
In Deuteronomy, as the Levites call out each line, the Torah says: "And all the people shall answer and say, Amen."
To say amen is to say: this holds, I'll stand on it. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, reads amen as the first letters of El melech ne'eman: God, faithful King.
And in tractate Berakhot it goes further: the one who answers amen is greater than the one who says the blessing. Third, the craftsman.
In the Song of Songs, a lover's beauty is compared to the work of a skilled craftsman's hands, and the word for craftsman carries these letters too.
A craftsman is someone whose hands you can trust: the joint holds, the seam stays shut. Fourth, people.
In Numbers, God describes Moses as one "who is faithful in all mine house." Faithful is ne'eman, the same root: not a person with no doubts, but a person who can be relied on.
So faith, read through these letters, leans less toward certainty and more toward reliability: hands that stay up, a word that holds, work that doesn't come apart.

how: Jews answer amen when they hear a blessing said by someone else, in synagogue and at the table, and the Talmud treats answering amen with care as a practice in its own right.

o: a root for certainty, belief with no doubts
a word meaning the end, said to close a prayer
the root of faith, amen and steadiness

games.q: the letters alef, mem, nun — tap the pairs.
p: said in answer to a blessing

s: in the battle story, emunah describes what Moses believed
it describes his hands: they were steady until sunset, held up by Aaron and Hur.
the Talmud says the one who answers amen is greater than the one who blesses
in Deuteronomy, amen is said by the one who speaks the words
"all the people shall answer and say, Amen." amen is an answer.

games.q: you're Aaron. Moses' arms are dropping, and each time they drop, the battle turns. what do you do?
o: bring a stone for him to sit on, and hold his hands up.
take his place on the hill.
games.why: Aaron and Hur sat him on a stone and held his hands, one on each side. then his hands were steady until sunset. the steadiness came from friends.

practice: Let your hands rest open and bring to mind one thing that has held for you: a person who keeps showing up, a habit that keeps you upright, a promise someone kept.
Stay with it for a few breaths, then say one word, quietly or just inside: amen, not as an ending but as a yes. If you pray, you can answer amen to a blessing you know, slowly, meaning each sound.

wordCard.voice: A-M-N. Alef, mem, nun: the letters of emunah, faith and steadiness; of amen, this holds; and of the craftsman whose work holds. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: faith, steadiness; from the letters alef, mem, nun, the letters of amen.

carryVoice: Your line: faith is steadiness. Amen isn't a full stop; it's a yes. See you tomorrow.
